segments: The seventeenth discourse.
[... including] Otkin {OCR?} Tūmān,
together with the rest of the sons of his uncles and his kinsmen, he sent to the country of the Cathayans.
Concerning the laws which Genghis
Khan established: Since the Mongols had no script or writing,
this Genghis Khan commanded the Uyghur scribes,
and they taught their script to the sons of the Tatars,
and they began writing the Mongol language in Uyghur script,
just as the Egyptians [write] in Greek,
and the Persians in Arabic.
He also commanded, and these laws which he established were written down:
First, that when they write any letter to rebels or send an envoy,
they should not threaten them with the greatness of their strength and their number,
but should only say:
"If you submit,
you will find goodness and rest;
and if you resist,
what do we know? The eternal God knows what will happen to you."
And in this way their reliance on the Lord is shown,
and for this reason they have conquered and conquer.
Second:
That the continent, the pure, the just, the scribes, and the wise men of any nation whatsoever, they shall magnify and honor;
and the wicked and unjust they shall hate.
And since they saw chastity and these other virtues more in the Christian people,
them they loved more at the beginning of their kingdom, but
only for a short time;
suddenly their love turned into hatred,
so that they cannot even bear to look upon them with their eyes,
because they all together have converted to Islam, the myriads of the people and the nations.
Third:
That to their kings and nobles,
they should not give many titles of praise like other nations,
especially the Muslims;
and to him who sits upon the throne of the kingdom they should add only one title:
"Khan" or "Qan";
and his brothers and kinsmen they should call by his original name, that of his birth.
Fourth: When they are unoccupied by war with enemies,
they should occupy themselves with hunting,
and teach their sons how to hunt wild animals,
so that they may be trained in warfare,
and acquire strength and endurance against hardship,
and encounter their enemies as [they do] savage beasts, and show no pity.
Fifth:
Fighting men from twenty years old and above:
for every ten there shall be one chief,
and for every hundred a chief,
and for every thousand a chief,
and for every myriad a chief.
Sixth:
The entire people
